subject: Increasing number of sites surveyed through time

messages.subject: Increasing number of sites surveyed through time
parts:
Hi unmarked users,

This is more of a general occupancy modeling question, not related to program unmarked. 

Throughout my study, the number of sites increased as new areas became available for surveying (through increased funding/personnel/etc.). I start with ~35 sites, then after a few years to ~60, then a few years later up to ~75. For those of you a bit more statistically savvy: can you forsee any potential pitfalls (ex. bias in parm estimates) from such a substantial change in sample size through time? Would there be advantages to maintaining a relatively stable number of sites surveyed in occupancy studies?

Thanks everyone,
Gavin

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Increasing number of sites surveyed through time
parts:
Hi Gavin,

in principle, if your sites in every year represent a random sample from the same statistical population of sites, then I would not see any problems: you simply increase the sample size and should get increasingly precise estimates.

However, it may well be that the decision to include a site in the sample is not independent from its state of occurrence. For instance, perhaps people start with surveying the best sites only and then later include also sites with less good habitat quality. The latter may naturally have a lower probability of being occupied, greater extinction and lower colonisation rates. If this is the case, then such a sampling design will yield an automatic "decline" of the species over time or will underestimate any increase.

There is one little caveat in addition: my colleague Arco van Strien from the Netherlands, who uses dynamic occupancy models a lot for inference about data from citizen-science programs, has told me that he found some bias in some estimators of the model related to changing numbers of missing values in a data matrix. Of course this is exactly what you will get when your sample size of sites changes over time. I can't remember the details, but perhaps you may want to run a little simulation study to check.

This is a general suggestion: analysing simulated data is incredibly powerful for quickly getting an intuition about things such as the design of a study, the quality of estimators or the estimability of parameters.

Kind regards --- Marc
